Sprechen is the A1 anchor verb behind every "do you speak ___?" question. It has a vowel change in the du form (du sprichst, e → i) but the Sie form is regular (Sie sprechen) and matches third-person plural — at A1 you can stay safe with the Sie form everywhere in service contexts.

Entschuldigung is the A1 polite gating word for any small interruption — opening a question, asking for a repeat, or repairing a misunderstanding. Grammatically a feminine noun (die Entschuldigung, "an apology") but used here as a fixed interjection. The slightly more formal alternative is Verzeihung; both are safe in service contexts.

Bahnhof is the A1 anchor compound noun for train travel: Bahn (rail) + Hof (yard) → train station. Masculine — der Bahnhof. Plural is irregular with umlaut + e: die Bahnhöfe. Once you know der Bahnhof you instantly recognise der Hauptbahnhof (main station) and der Busbahnhof (bus station).

Möchte is the A1 polite-conditional form for ordering and requesting anywhere in a German-speaking country. It is socially softer than "Ich will" ("I want"), which is grammatically simpler but feels blunt in service. Note the case shift on the noun: der Kaffee (Nominativ) becomes einen Kaffee (Akkusativ) as the direct object of möchte. Umlauts unavailable on a keyboard? Standard substitute is "moechte".

Kostet is the A1 verb form behind every price question in German shops, markets, and cafés. The verb kosten is regular (ich koste, du kostest, es kostet). Modern spelling is two words — Wie viel — though older texts sometimes show "Wieviel" collapsed.

Zug is the A1 anchor noun for train travel anywhere German is spoken. Masculine — der Zug. Plural is irregular with umlaut + e: die Züge. The preposition "nach" with city names takes Dativ but no article: nach Berlin, never "nach dem Berlin".

Hilfe is the A1 anchor noun for any open help request. Feminine — die Hilfe. Used here as the direct object of brauche, but feminine singular looks identical in Nominativ and Akkusativ, so the form does not change. Pair with brauchen (to need) — both A1 core. Useful as a one-word call in emergencies.

Schön is the A1 anchor adjective that works for places (schön hier), people (sehr schön), weather (Es ist schön draußen), and as a standalone polite acknowledgement (Schön!). The ö is a true umlaut: where umlauts are not available on a keyboard, the standard substitute is "schoen", not "schon" (which is a different A1 word meaning "already").

Morgen is the A1 time anchor for next-day planning. Watch the capitalisation rule: lowercase "morgen" is the adverb ("tomorrow"); capitalised "Morgen" is the masculine noun (der Morgen, "morning"). At the start of a sentence either version looks capitalised. Pairs cleanly with "Perfekt" as a beginner-safe affirmation.

Wiedersehen is the A1 anchor inside the formal goodbye Auf Wiedersehen — a neuter compound noun (das Wiedersehen = wieder "again" + sehen "to see"). On the phone, Germans say Auf Wiederhören ("hearing again") instead. The casual peer equivalent is Tschüss.

Verstehe is the A1 anchor first-person form of verstehen. The verb takes no separable prefix here (it is ver- + stehen, an inseparable prefix that stays attached). Negation pattern: nicht follows the verb in main clauses — Ich verstehe nicht, not "Ich nicht verstehe". The Dativ mir in helfen Sie mir is required: helfen always governs the Dativ object.

Aufschreiben is the A1 anchor for an A1 separable verb (auf- + schreiben). In a main clause the prefix detaches and goes to the end — Schreiben Sie das auf. In a modal + infinitive construction (Können Sie das aufschreiben?) the verb stays joined as one infinitive. Same pattern as aufmachen (open), aufstehen (get up), einkaufen (shop).

Zeigen is the A1 anchor verb for showing or pointing — used with two objects: a Dativ person (mir = to me) and an Akkusativ thing (das = it). Note the case shift on Karte: die Karte (Nominativ) becomes der Karte after the preposition auf when the meaning is location (Dativ). For direction-to instead of location, auf would take Akkusativ — but at A1 the map case is consistently Dativ.

Besser is the A1 anchor comparative form — gut → besser → am besten (good, better, best). It is irregular: a stem-changing comparative, not "guter" (which would be wrong). German short comparatives end in -er like in English: schnell → schneller, klein → kleiner, but gut goes to besser. Dieses (this, neuter) and das (that, neuter) are deictic demonstratives — point physically to make the choice clear.

Gibt is the A1 anchor form behind the existential idiom es gibt — "there is / there are" — used to talk about availability and presence. Literally "it gives", but functionally equivalent to English "there is". Pair: Es gibt Brot (There is bread) / Gibt es Brot? (Is there bread?). At A1 the object after es gibt is always Akkusativ (es gibt einen Kaffee), but in the deictic short form Gibt es das? the das is unmarked.

Zahlen is the A1 anchor verb for paying — used in restaurants (Ich möchte zahlen) and shops (Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?). Note: bezahlen is the closely related variant (with the inseparable be- prefix), also A1, used the same way. The noun Karte (f.) is dual-use in German: card (EC-Karte, Kreditkarte) and map (Stadtkarte). Context disambiguates; here mit Karte clearly means card.

Quittung is the A1 anchor for the printed receipt in any German shop or restaurant. Feminine — die Quittung. Plural: die Quittungen. The related word Rechnung is more common in restaurants and for bills (Die Rechnung, bitte. = The bill, please), while Quittung is the printed proof of payment in retail. The bag word Tüte (f., die Tüte) is the standard A1 carrier — Plastiktüte (plastic bag) and Papiertüte (paper bag) are common compounds.

Reservierung is the A1 anchor noun for a booking at restaurants or services. Feminine — die Reservierung. Plural: die Reservierungen. As the direct object of habe it is in Akkusativ, but feminine singular Nom/Akk look identical so the article stays eine. The borrowed verb reservieren (to reserve) is the matching action. For hotels the more specific compound is Zimmerreservierung (room reservation).

Richtig is the A1 anchor adjective for "correct" — used as a predicate (Das ist richtig) and as a standalone affirmation (Richtig!). The opposite is falsch. As a predicate adjective it takes no ending — just bare richtig. Adverb use is identical in form (Du sprichst richtig = You speak correctly), so no -ly suffix is needed.

Moment is the A1 anchor noun for asking briefly to wait. Masculine — der Moment. As the direct object of an implied verb (here, the elliptical Geben Sie mir...) it is in Akkusativ, hence einen Moment (der → einen). A common A1 alternative is Eine Sekunde (Sekunde is feminine, so eine instead of einen). The shortest form Einen Augenblick is also A1 — Augenblick literally "eye-glance" (Auge + Blick).

Rechts is the A1 direction word for "right". It is an adverb (so no -e adjective ending) and pairs naturally with links (left) and geradeaus (straight ahead). Do not confuse with the homonym recht in phrases like Du hast recht ("You are right" = correct) — context disambiguates. The fixed phrase nach rechts (to the right) uses Akkusativ-governing nach.

Weit is the A1 anchor adjective for distance. Used as a predicate (Ist es weit?), and with noch (Ist es noch weit? — Is it still far?). Its opposite is nah (near, A1). The adverb form is identical to the adjective. False-friend warning: weit is not "wait" (English wait is warten in German).

Geöffnet is the A1 anchor past participle of öffnen ("to open"), used adjectivally to describe a place that is currently open for business. The plain adjective offen is also A1 and means the same thing in this context — Das Café ist offen / geöffnet. The opposite is geschlossen (past part. of schließen) or zu (short form). The ö is a true umlaut: with no keyboard for it, type "geoeffnet".

Welcher is the A1 anchor interrogative determiner — like English "which", but it agrees with the noun in gender and case. Masculine Nom: welcher (welcher Bus, welcher Mann), feminine Nom: welche (welche Karte), neuter Nom: welches (welches Buch). The contracted zum = zu + dem (zu always takes Dativ) and matches the masculine Hauptbahnhof.

Nächste is the A1 anchor adjective for "next" — derived from nah ("near") via the superlative (am nächsten). Here it shows the weak adjective ending: after the definite article die, the feminine Nominativ adjective ending is -e (die nächste). With der it would be der nächste (m, Nom weak); with das, das nächste; with no article, nächste (strong). Pair it with Haltestelle for transit and with Mal (das Mal, "time/occasion") for nächstes Mal ("next time").

Fahrkarte is the A1 anchor compound noun for a transit ticket: Fahr- (from fahren "to go/ride") + Karte (card). Feminine — die Fahrkarte. Plural: die Fahrkarten. The shorter borrowed Ticket (das Ticket, n.) is also A1 and is now common at machines and airports. For a one-way ticket, add einfach (Eine einfache Fahrkarte / einfache Fahrt); for return, hin und zurück.

Schließt is the A1 anchor 3rd-person singular of schließen ("to close"). It teaches two German features at once: stem change (ie → ie holds in schließen; no ablaut for present tense) and the ß rule — after a long vowel, German uses ß (schließen, schließt). In Swiss German only ss is used. The acceptedAnswers tolerate schliesst as a common-keyboard alternative. Opposite: öffnet (3rd-p sg of öffnen).

Ecke is the A1 anchor noun for a street corner. Feminine — die Ecke. Plural: die Ecken. Used here in the Dativ after an (a "two-way preposition" — Dativ for location, Akkusativ for direction). At a corner = an der Ecke; toward the corner = an die Ecke. A1-safe partner: die Straße (the street).

Fuß is the A1 anchor noun for the body part — and the core word inside the fixed idiom zu Fuß ("on foot"). Masculine — der Fuß. Plural: die Füße (umlaut + e). The ß after the long u is the standard spelling — Swiss German would write Fuss, so acceptedAnswers tolerate that. zu Fuß never takes an article and is a frozen prepositional idiom. The plural Füße appears in many compound idioms (die kalten Füße bekommen — to get cold feet).

Haltestelle is the A1 anchor compound noun for a transit stop: Halte- (from halten "to stop, to hold") + Stelle ("place"). Feminine — die Haltestelle. Plural: die Haltestellen. Used in this lesson as the direct object of verpasst — feminine singular Nom/Akk look identical, so the article stays die. The construction Ich habe ... verpasst is the A1 perfect tense (haben + past participle) — common spoken past for completed actions.

Tisch is the A1 anchor noun for any dining table. Masculine — der Tisch. Plural: die Tische. As the direct object of the implicit ich möchte it shifts from der to einen (m, Akk). The preposition für always takes Akkusativ, but zwei is a number with no article so case is invisible. At A1 numbers 1-12 are essential — eins, zwei, drei.

Speisekarte is the A1 anchor compound for a restaurant menu: Speise (dish) + Karte (card). Feminine — die Speisekarte. Plural: die Speisekarten. The shorter Karte alone also works in context (Die Karte, bitte.). Distinct from Getränkekarte (drinks menu). The implicit Akkusativ as direct object of the elliptical ich möchte is form-identical to Nominativ for feminine nouns, so the article stays die.

Tee is the A1 anchor noun for tea — straightforward masculine, der Tee. Plural die Tees is rarely needed at A1. The earlier P1 lesson taught Kaffee with möchte and einen; this lesson repeats the same template with a new noun and the same Akkusativ pattern (der Tee → einen Tee). Useful pairings: schwarzer Tee (black tea), grüner Tee (green tea), Pfefferminztee (peppermint tea).

Ohne is the A1 anchor preposition for "without" — it always takes Akkusativ. Masculine objects shift: der Zucker → ohne Zucker (masc. Akk = den/einen, but Zucker is uncountable here so no article). Opposite: mit ("with"), which takes Dativ — same uncountable Zucker stays bare in both directions. Useful pairings: ohne Milch (without milk), ohne Eis (without ice), ohne mich (without me — the personal pronoun also flips: ich → mich in Akk).

Frisch is the A1 anchor adjective for "fresh" — used for food (frisches Brot, frische Milch), air (frische Luft), and weather (es ist frisch — "it is cool"). As a predicate adjective after sein it takes no ending. The adverb form is identical. False-friend warning: frisch is not "fresh" in the slang English sense (cheeky/bold); the German for that is dreist or unverschämt.

Nichts is the A1 anchor negative indefinite pronoun for "nothing". Pair with mehr ("more / else") for the canonical "nothing else" close: nichts mehr. Useful pairings: nichts zu trinken (nothing to drink), nichts Neues (nothing new), gar nichts (nothing at all). Distinct from kein/keine (which negate a noun directly — Ich habe kein Geld).

Mitnehmen is an A1 separable verb — mit- + nehmen ("to take"). In a main clause the prefix detaches and goes to the end: Ich nehme das mit. In a modal + infinitive construction (Ich möchte das mitnehmen) the verb stays joined. In the fixed phrase zum Mitnehmen ("for taking away"), Mitnehmen is a nominalized infinitive — capitalised like a noun, neuter (das Mitnehmen). The opposite at A1 service is zum Hieressen / Hier essen ("to eat in").

Lecker is the A1 anchor adjective for food praise — used as predicate (Das ist lecker) and attributively (lecker, but no -er when used predicatively). Often heard as a standalone exclamation: Lecker! For drinks the more natural alternative is gut (Das war gut). The past tense war comes from sein ("to be") — one of the most irregular German verbs (Präteritum): ich war, du warst, er war, wir waren, sie waren, Sie waren.

Wetter is the A1 anchor noun for weather. Neuter — das Wetter (no plural at A1). The phrase schönes Wetter shows the strong adjective ending -es: when no article precedes the noun, the adjective itself carries the case/gender/number marking (here neuter Nominativ → -es). The tag oder at the end is the German equivalent of English "right?" or "isn’t it?" — a soft conversational hook.

Rechnung is the A1 anchor noun for the restaurant bill. Feminine — die Rechnung. Plural: die Rechnungen. Distinct from Quittung (printed shop receipt, P2 trophy) — in restaurants you get a Rechnung, in shops you get a Quittung. Useful add-ons at the table: zusammen (together — all on one bill) and getrennt (separately — split). For a fixed amount tip you say a rounded number to the server: Stimmt so ("keep the change") for the full amount.

Spät is the A1 anchor adjective and adverb for "late". As an adverb after sein it takes no ending: Ich bin spät. With the intensifier zu it becomes Ich bin zu spät (too late).
